title: CS 3810 — Computer Organization
summary: 11 assignments spanning performance analysis, MIPS assembly, digital logic, assembler design, pipelining, and cache optimization for CS 3810

data.text: A comprehensive tour through computer organization for CS 3810 at the University of Utah across 11 assignments (Spring 2025), progressing from high-level performance metrics and number representations down through MIPS assembly programming, digital logic design, a custom two-pass assembler written in Python, pipeline hazard analysis, and finally cache simulation and optimization. Each assignment peeled back another layer of abstraction — from reasoning about CPI and Amdahl's Law, to hand-encoding machine instructions, to writing recursive MIPS with full callee-save stack discipline, to building an assembler that turns human-readable mnemonics into binary, to designing caches that minimize miss rates on real workloads. Written submissions were typeset in LaTeX, assembly was tested in MARS 4.5, circuits were built in a digital logic simulator, and the Python projects ranged from a regex-driven assembler to a brute-force cache parameter optimizer.

items.content: CPI, clock rate, and IPS analysis: compared three processors (P1 at 3 GHz, P2 at 2.5 GHz, P3 at 4 GHz) across different instruction-class mixes, computing cycles-per-instruction weighted by class frequencies and deriving instructions-per-second to identify which processor actually executes a given workload fastest despite having a slower clock

Clock cycle reduction: analyzed a proposed CPI improvement for P1 (reducing CPI of class A from 1→2 cycles while lowering clock time to 0.5 ns), calculated execution time before and after the change, and determined the net speedup — illustrating that a higher CPI can still win if the clock period shrinks enough

Amdahl's Law: applied the speedup formula to determine how much of an overall program must be improved to hit a target speedup, reinforcing the diminishing-returns insight that accelerating 10% of a workload can never yield more than ~1.11× overall

Manufacturing yield: calculated die area, dies per wafer, and defect-driven yield for a 300 mm wafer at a given defect density, then explored how shrinking the die or reducing defects shifts the cost-per-good-die equation
Number base conversions: converted a student ID (u1480977) into 32-bit binary and hexadecimal representations as a warmup for the representation-heavy work in A2

Three-way hex interpretation: took raw hex values and decoded them as unsigned integer, two's complement signed integer, and IEEE 754 single-precision float — the same bit pattern yielding three completely different numbers depending on the interpretation scheme
Overflow detection: built truth tables for addition overflow under both unsigned and two's complement, identifying carry-out vs. sign-bit disagreement as the distinguishing detection mechanisms

Decimal to IEEE 754 conversion: manually converted decimal values (including negatives and fractions) into 32-bit IEEE 754 — decomposing sign, biased exponent (bias 127), and normalized mantissa with the implicit leading 1

Custom 16-bit float design: designed a reduced-precision float format with 1 sign bit, 5 exponent bits (bias 15), and 10 mantissa bits, then analyzed its range and precision tradeoffs compared to IEEE 754 single-precision

Precision boundary: proved that 224 (16,777,216) is the largest integer exactly representable in IEEE 754 single-precision by showing that 224+1 requires 25 significand bits but only 24 are available (23 stored + 1 implicit)

Mystery program analysis: reverse-engineered a MIPS program that computes floor(n/3) without using division — it doubles the input, then counts how many times it can subtract 6, effectively implementing integer division through repeated subtraction on a scaled value

C-to-MIPS translation: hand-translated C functions into MIPS assembly, mapping local variables to registers, array accesses to base-plus-offset lw/sw instructions with sll for word-aligned indexing, and if/else branches to beq/bne with labels

Register allocation: practiced mapping C variables to MIPS registers ($t0–$t9 for temporaries, $s0–$s7 for saved values), choosing which values survive across function calls and which can be freely overwritten

Absolute value without pseudoinstructions: implemented abs(n) using only real MIPS instructions — XOR with 0xFFFFFFFF to flip all bits, then add 1 to complete the two's complement negation, with a branch to skip negation for non-negative inputs

Formula via strength reduction: computed 9x + 5 using only add/addi — no multiply instruction — by chaining x → 2x → 4x → 8x → 9x through repeated doubling, demonstrating how compilers replace expensive multiplications with shift-add sequences
Bit isolation: extracted the bit at position x from integer n using srav (arithmetic right shift by x) followed by andi with 1, plus input validation ensuring x stays within [0, 31]

Range summation loop: summed all integers in [x, y] using slt and bne for loop control, accumulating into a register and printing the result with a syscall — straightforward loop mechanics but a key exercise in MIPS branching idioms

Full recursive mergesort: implemented a complete mergesort in MIPS assembly with 24-byte stack frames that save $ra and $s0–$s4 on every recursive call, compute mid = left + (right − left) / 2 via srl, recursively sort both halves, then merge in-place — the most complex assembly program in the course

Stack discipline: practiced the MIPS calling convention end-to-end — callee-saved registers pushed on entry and popped on exit, arguments passed in $a0–$a3, return values in $v0, and $sp adjusted symmetrically so the stack unwinds correctly through O(n log n) recursive depth

Power-of-2 filter: wrote a function that scans an array and copies only power-of-2 elements into a result array, detecting powers of 2 by right-shifting until 1 and checking that no other bits were set — using proper jal/jr calling convention with $ra preservation

R-type and I-type encoding: hand-encoded MIPS instructions into 32-bit binary by filling in opcode, rs, rt, rd, shamt, and funct fields for R-type, and opcode, rs, rt, and immediate fields for I-type — then decoded hex machine words back into assembly mnemonics

Combinational logic design: built truth tables from English specifications, derived sum-of-products Boolean expressions, and simplified them — translating word-problem requirements into minimal gate-level circuits

Finite state machine: designed a conveyor-belt controller FSM with states, transitions, and output logic, specifying the state diagram, transition table, and the flip-flop/gate implementation needed to build it in hardware

Digital circuit implementation: designed and built circuits in a logic simulator (.cv format), wiring gates, flip-flops, and multiplexers to implement the combinational and sequential logic from A6's theoretical designs

Iterative refinement: multiple circuit file versions (structured vs. unstructured layouts) reflect the process of reorganizing wiring for clarity and correctness — mirroring real hardware design iteration

Two-pass assembly: built a complete assembler for the COAL instruction set architecture — pass one scans for labels and records their addresses in a symbol table, pass two resolves label references and emits binary machine code

16-bit ISA with 13 instructions: the COAL architecture uses 4-bit opcodes, 2-bit register fields (4 registers: R0–R3), and multiple instruction formats — R-type (register-register), I-type (register-immediate), J-type (jump with 12-bit address), and H-type (halt)

Regex-driven parsing: used Python regular expressions to tokenize each assembly line, handling LW/SW offset syntax (e.g., LW R1, 4(R2)) with a dedicated regex pattern that extracts the offset and base register separately

Label resolution: forward references (jumping to a label defined later in the source) work automatically because pass one builds the full symbol table before pass two emits any code — a textbook demonstration of why assemblers need multiple passes

CLI with argparse: the assembler runs from the command line, taking an input .asm file and producing a binary output file, with proper error handling for unknown instructions, undefined labels, and malformed operands

Single-cycle vs. pipelined timing: calculated execution time for instruction sequences under both models, demonstrating how pipelining overlaps stages (IF → ID → EX → MEM → WB) to achieve near-N× speedup for N-stage pipes on long instruction streams

Data hazard analysis: traced register dependencies through pipeline stages to identify read-after-write (RAW) hazards, then compared three resolution strategies: stalling (inserting bubbles), forwarding/bypassing (routing results directly from EX/MEM to the next instruction's inputs), and a combination of both

Control hazards: analyzed branch instructions in the pipeline, computing the penalty of mispredicted branches and the cycles lost to pipeline flushes when a branch resolves in the MEM stage vs. the ID stage

Instruction reordering: optimized code sequences by rearranging independent instructions to fill branch delay slots and eliminate data-hazard stalls — a manual version of what modern compilers do automatically to maximize pipeline throughput

Speedup calculations: computed actual speedup ratios (pipelined vs. single-cycle) for specific instruction traces, accounting for stall cycles, forwarding paths, and branch penalties — showing that real speedup falls short of the ideal N× due to hazards

Three associativity modes: implemented direct-mapped, set-associative, and fully-associative caches in a single Python simulator, switching behavior based on the number of sets and ways specified at runtime

Address decomposition: split each memory address into tag, index, and offset fields based on cache geometry (block size determines offset bits, number of sets determines index bits, remaining bits form the tag) — the fundamental operation underlying all cache lookups

LRU replacement: tracked access recency using ordered lists within a dictionary, evicting the least-recently-used block when a set is full — a faithful simulation of the replacement policy used in real hardware

Storage overhead calculation: computed the total SRAM cost of each cache configuration including tag storage, valid bits, and LRU tracking bits alongside the data storage — showing that higher associativity adds metadata overhead that must be weighed against the miss-rate improvement

Brute-force parameter search: refactored the A10 simulator to sweep 280 cache configurations — block sizes from 64 B to 1024 B, set counts from 2 to 128, associativity from 1-way to 8-way — against a 464 KB memory-address trace from a ray-tracing workload

BVH traversal analysis: analyzed why the ray-tracing workload benefits from large cache lines (256 B) — bounding-volume hierarchy (BVH) node traversals access spatially adjacent memory, so wider lines capture more of the access pattern in each fetch and dramatically cut compulsory misses

Optimal configuration: identified 256 B lines, 2 sets, 4-way associativity as the best large-cache design for this workload, achieving the lowest miss rate while staying within the bit budget — a result that contradicts the naive assumption that more sets always help

LaTeX report: wrote up the optimization methodology, results tables, and analysis as a formal technical report in LaTeX, explaining why spatial locality in BVH traversals makes line size the dominant parameter and why the optimal set count is surprisingly low

Recursive MIPS stack management: mergesort required tracking five callee-saved values ($s0–$s4 plus $ra) across recursive calls that go O(log n) deep — one misaligned $sp adjustment or forgotten restore would corrupt the entire call tree; solved by templating a strict 24-byte frame and verifying with MARS single-step execution

Two-pass assembler label resolution: forward references to labels not yet defined required separating scanning (pass 1) from code generation (pass 2) — initially tried a single-pass approach that broke on forward jumps, then restructured into the classic two-pass design where pass 1 builds a complete symbol table before pass 2 emits any binary

LW/SW offset parsing: the LW R1, 4(R2) syntax doesn't tokenize cleanly with split() — solved with a dedicated regex r'(\d+)\((R[0-3])\)' that captures the numeric offset and base register as separate groups, handling the parenthesized addressing mode the ISA spec requires

Pipeline trace accuracy: hand-tracing 10+ instructions through a 5-stage pipeline with forwarding paths and branch penalties required meticulous cycle-by-cycle bookkeeping — developed a tabular method (instruction × cycle grid) to systematically track which stage each instruction occupies and where forwarding eliminates stalls

Cache simulator correctness: off-by-one errors in address-bit decomposition (particularly the boundary between index and tag fields) caused phantom misses in set-associative mode — debugged by printing the tag/index/offset split for known addresses and cross-checking against hand calculations

MIPS assembly: register allocation, memory addressing modes (base+offset), control flow (branches, jumps), bit manipulation (shifts, masks, XOR), recursive functions with full callee-save stack frames, and the MIPS calling convention

Computer arithmetic: unsigned and two's complement integer representation, IEEE 754 single-precision floating point, overflow detection, precision boundaries, and custom reduced-precision float design
Performance analysis: CPI calculation, clock rate vs. throughput tradeoffs, Amdahl's Law, and manufacturing yield modeling — the quantitative tools for evaluating architectural decisions
Digital logic: truth tables, sum-of-products expressions, Boolean simplification, finite state machines, and circuit implementation in a logic simulator
Instruction encoding: R-type and I-type MIPS instruction formats, hand encoding/decoding between assembly and 32-bit binary, and the relationship between ISA design and hardware decoder complexity
Assembler construction: two-pass assembly, symbol tables, label resolution, regex-based tokenization, and the translation from mnemonic instructions to binary machine code

Pipelining: 5-stage pipeline operation (IF/ID/EX/MEM/WB), data hazards and RAW dependencies, stalling vs. forwarding/bypassing, control hazards, branch delay slots, and instruction reordering for hazard elimination

Cache architecture: direct-mapped, set-associative, and fully-associative designs, LRU replacement, address decomposition (tag/index/offset), storage overhead analysis, and workload-driven parameter optimization
Python tooling: building command-line tools (argparse), regex-driven parsing, dictionary-based data structures for symbol tables and LRU tracking, and brute-force search over parameter spaces
LaTeX: typesetting technical documents with mathematical notation, tables, code listings, and structured reports for both homework submissions and the cache optimization analysis
